💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding.
  • The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines.
  • Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding. It’s purpose-built for reliable information extraction from complex documents, forms, and structured visuals. Granite 4.0 3B Vision excels on the following capabilities:.

The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines. It continues to support vision-language tasks such as producing detailed natural-language descriptions from images (e.g., “Describe this image in detail”). The model can be used standalone or in tandem with Docling to enhance document processing pipelines with deep visual understanding capabilities.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.

It has been revealed that charts present a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs) because understanding them requires jointly reasoning over visual patterns, numerical data, and natural language, a combination most VLMs cannot handle well, especially when spatial precision matters—such as reading exact values off a line chart. To close this gap, we’ve developed ChartNet: a million-scale multimodal dataset purpose-built for chart interpretation and reasoning, described in detail in our upcoming CVPR 2026 paper.

Recent findings suggest that chartNet uses a code-guided synthesis pipeline to generate 1.7 million diverse chart samples spanning 24 chart types and 6 plotting libraries [see Figure 1]. What makes it so distinctive is that each sample consists of five aligned components—plotting code, rendered image, data table, natural language summary, and QA pairs—providing models a deeply cross-modal view of what a chart means, not just what it looks like. The dataset also includes human-annotated and real-world subsets, filtered for visual fidelity, semantic accuracy, and diversity.

The result is a training resource that moves VLMs from merely describing charts to genuinely understanding the structured information they encode—with consistent gains across model sizes, architectures, and tasks.

Figure 1: ChartNet’s synthetic data generation pipeline.

Most VLMs inject visual information into their language model at a single point, which forces the model to handle both high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial detail simultaneously. Granite 4.0 3B Vision takes a different approach with DeepStack Injection: abstract visual features are routed into earlier layers for semantic understanding, while high-resolution spatial features are fed into later layers to preserve detail. The result is a model that understands both what is in a document and where—which is critical for tasks like table extraction, chart understanding, and KVP parsing where layout matters as much as content. For a full technical breakdown, see the Model Architecture section of the model card.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision is packaged as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, rather than as a standalone model. In practice, this means the same deployment can serve both multimodal and text-only workloads, automatically falling back to the base model when vision isn’t required. This keeps enterprise integration straightforward without sacrificing performance.

Charts: Evaluated on the human-verified ChartNet benchmark using LLM-as-a-judge, Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the highest Chart2Summary (86.4%) score among all evaluated models, including significantly larger ones [see Figure 2]. It also ranks second on Chart2CSV (62.1%), behind only Qwen3.5-9B (63.4%), a model more than double its size.

Figure 2: Granite 4.0 3B Vision performance on chart2csv and chart2summary, compared against peer vision-language models using LLM-as-a-judge.

Tables: We evaluate table extraction in two settings: cropped tables (isolated regions) and full-page documents (tables embedded in complex layouts) [see Figure 3]. The benchmark suite includes TableVQA-extract (cropped table images), OmniDocBench-tables (full-page documents), and PubTables-v2 (both cropped and full-page settings). Models are tasked with extracting tables in HTML format and scored using TEDS, a metric that captures both structural and content accuracy. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the strongest performance across benchmarks, leading on PubTablesV2 on both cropped (92.1) and full-page (79.3), OmniDocBench (64.0), and TableVQA (88.1) scores among all evaluated models.

Figure 3: Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s table extraction performance across cropped and full-page benchmarks (TableVQA-extract, PubTables-v2, OmniDocBench-tables), measured by TEDS.

Sources indicate that semantic KVP: VAREX is a benchmark specifically designed to discriminate between small extraction models, comprising 1,777 U.S. government forms spanning simple flat layouts to complex nested and tabular structures. Models are evaluated using exact match (EM), a strict metric that requires the model’s extracted key-value pairs to match the ground truth. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves 85.5% EM accuracy zero-shot.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision can operate either as a stand‑alone visual information extraction engine or as part of a fully automated document‑processing pipeline with Docling. The model is designed to support scalable, accurate extraction across diverse document types and visual formats.

1. Stand‑Alone Image Understanding Granite 4.0 3B Vision can run directly on individual images, making this option useful for applications with existing workflows that need targeted visual extraction without modifying upstream systems. This offers easy integration into existing automation workflows and is suitable for lightweight, task‑specific tools (e.g., form parsers, chart analyzers, etc.).

2. Integrated Document Understanding Pipeline With Docling Granite 4.0 3B Vision can also be integrated seamlessly with Docling to support complete end‑to‑end document understanding. This mode can offer:.

Sources indicate that granite 4.0 3B Vision is available now on HuggingFace, released under the Apache 2.0 license. Full technical details, training methodology, and benchmark results are available in the model card. We’d love to hear what you build with it—share your feedback in the community tab.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense.
  • The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s strategy to launch a million datacenter satellites.
  • The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense.

The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s strategy to launch a million datacenter satellites.

The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”.

The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the firm to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union.

SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less.

Elon Musk’s company asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.”.

The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request.

“SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The tech giant must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters.

Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions.

Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “peak insanity.”.

In a recent development, google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily rolls out, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so.

Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create.

Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant latest fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained.

Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites.

Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having launched a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029.

Sources indicate that down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India currently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A few weeks ago, we wrote about one-shotting full web apps with gr.HTML: building rich, interactive frontends entirely inside Gradio using custom HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. That unlocked a lot. But what if that's not enough?

What if you want to build with your own frontend framework entirely like React, Svelte, or even plain HTML/JS, while still benefiting from Gradio's queuing system, API infrastructure, MCP support, and ZeroGPU on Spaces?

That's exactly the problem gradio.Server solves. And it changes what's possible with Gradio and Hugging Face Spaces.

It has been revealed that text Behind Image : an editor where you upload a photo, the background gets removed using an ML model, and then you place stylized text between the foreground subject and the background. The text appears to sit behind the person or object in the image.

There's no way to express this UI in Gradio components. It's a full web application. But We still wanted the backend power of Gradio: queuing, concurrency management, ZeroGPU support, and hosting on HF Spaces without infrastructure headaches.

gradio.Server extends FastAPI. It gives you the full power of FastAPI (custom routes, middleware, file uploads, any response type) while adding Gradio's API engine on top: queuing, SSE streaming, concurrency control, and gradio_client compatibility.

Here's the entire backend for Text Behind Image:.

That's it. ~50 lines of Python. The model loads at startup, @spaces.GPU handles ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio.Server manages queuing and concurrency. Let's break down what's happening.

If this were a regular FastAPI app, you'd define a @app.post() route for background removal. That works, until two people hit it at once. Without concurrency management, both requests fight for the GPU, and the app crashes or returns garbage.

@app.api() solves this. It wraps your function with Gradio's queuing engine: requests are serialized, concurrency is controlled, and on ZeroGPU Spaces, GPU allocation is handled automatically via @spaces.GPU. As a bonus, any @app.api() endpoint is also callable via gradio_client, so other apps or scripts can use your Space programmatically:.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, @app.get("/") is a standard FastAPI route that serves the HTML page. Both coexist naturally because Server is a FastAPI app.

In a recent development, the index.html in this example is a self-contained ~1300-line web application. No React, no build step, no bundler. Just vanilla HTML with:.

The frontend talks to the backend using the Gradio JS Client:.

It has been revealed that this is the key part: by using the Gradio JS client rather than a raw fetch() call, the frontend goes through Gradio's queue. That means concurrency is managed, GPU requests don't collide, and you could even show queue position or progress to the user. Everything else, text rendering, layer compositing, export, happens in the browser.

Here's what was not possible before gradio.Server:.

With gradio.Server, Gradio doubles as a backend framework, use its UI system when you want it, bring your own frontend when you don't.

If you want Gradio's UI, you can use gr.Blocks, gr.Interface, gr.ChatInterface. If you want your own UI, use gradio.Server and bring whatever frontend you like. Either way, you get Spaces hosting, API queuing, gradio_client access, the full HF ecosystem, and more.

The app is live on Spaces: ysharma/text-behind-image.

According to recent reports, upload any photo with a clear subject, and start layering text behind it. Try the 3D extrusion, perspective tilt, and stroke effects, they combine nicely.

Industry observers note that this post covered the core idea: gradio.Server lets you pair any frontend with Gradio's backend. There's more to explore, including MCP tool registration with @app.mcp.tool(), SSE streaming for real-time updates, batch processing, and patterns for building multi-page apps with shared state.

According to recent reports, we'll dig into those in a follow-up post. Stay tuned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Indian politicians have proposed that AI could take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Machines of loving grace to turn social media grumps into services, finger painting into career advice.

Indian politicians have proposed that AI could take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers.

Industry observers note that modi suggested that parents of three-year-old children should enter data about their offspring’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system that is also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends. Those records, the PM suggested, will “help identify children's interests and aptitude from an early age and redirect them in the study of their choice in future.”.

That’s not an entirely creepy idea, because gaining access to India’s top tertiary institutions requires students to pay a hefty fee to sit for entrance exams. Modi pitched recommendations from the AI-powered app as something parents will appreciate as they contemplate whether to fund their offspring’s studies.

India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh (UP), has proposed to build an “AI Stack” to serve its 240 million-plus residents.

A 178-page tender seeks bidders to build a system that uses the state’s Family ID – a unique identifier for each household – to link data held by multiple agencies so it can be put to work in a dozen AI use cases.

One of those use cases is a tool for “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection” that “analyses publicly available social media content including online news channels and connected grievance channels to detect emerging urban complications, citizen complaints, service interruptions, and recurring service gaps.”.

In a recent development, the government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps.

Another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits.

Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes.

UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets.

India’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention notable oversight measures for the AI Stack. ®.

Falcon Perception

📅 01 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts.
  • We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.
  • This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

Many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a upcoming fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

It has been revealed that in our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

At its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

Images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:.

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

It has been revealed that dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) rapidly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:.

Recent findings suggest that this ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:.

Recent findings suggest that coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

Industry observers note that segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

Existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:.

Industry observers note that each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

Rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:.

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:.

We maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Sources indicate that stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question.".

In a recent development, stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:.

It has been revealed that on the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:.

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:.

This is where the early-fusion design shows the largest differences:.

Recent findings suggest that on simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:.

Industry observers note that "168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

"Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

According to recent reports, "Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

Industry observers note that modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

In a recent development, we took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

Recent findings suggest that we trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

Industry observers note that we train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

We evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

Industry observers note that at 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:.

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

More broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Click each category below to expand.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

In our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.).

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon.

Please check out the github repo for details.

According to recent reports, falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

The architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Unveiled on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

The headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.

According to recent reports, to make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting challenges on upgrade are advised to revision dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the fresh Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:.

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:.

The upcoming global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:.

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:.

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,.

you should immediately patch security advisories.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

Industry observers note that importStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an update could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.

Upgrading uses rustup update stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

Welcome Gemma 4: Frontier multimodal intelligence on device

📅 02 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.
  • Industry observers note that these models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device.
  • In a recent development, we collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.

Industry observers note that these models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

In a recent development, we collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:.

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

Industry observers note that as shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

In a recent development, the shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

We saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

For more details, check the Hugging Face on Microsoft Azure documentation.

Google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

Sources indicate that assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

The headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Sources indicate that benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:.

Sources indicate that for best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

Gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

According to recent reports, to showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

You can find the complete example in the "Hugging Face on Google Cloud" docs at https://hf.co/docs/google-cloud/examples/vertex-ai-notebooks-fine-tune-gemma-4.

Gemma 4 models demonstrate exceptional performance across diverse benchmarks, from reasoning and coding to vision and long-context tasks. The graph below shows model performance vs size, with Gemma 4 models forming an impressive Pareto frontier:.

one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's presently no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tempus AI entered a senior secured credit agreement on November 25, 2026, providing $385 million of term-loan commitments and $115 million of revolving commitments to help finance its pending Personalis acquisition, according to its Form 8-K.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate November 24, 2026 decision, Tempus elected to pay approximately $600 million in cash and issue approximately $900 million in Tempus Class A common stock to Personalis shareholders. These are financing commitments, not evidence that the full amounts have already been drawn. Initial funding requires the acquisition to have closed or be reasonably expected to close within one business day after funding.

Tempus expects borrowings to fund part of the acquisition consideration and related transaction costs, as well as working capital and general corporate purposes. Ares Capital Corporation is the administrative and collateral agent, Ares Capital Management LLC the lead arranger and bookrunner, and ACF Finco I LP the revolving agent.

According to recent reports, term loans bear interest at either the agreement’s Base Rate benchmark plus 4.50% or its Term SOFR benchmark plus 5.50%; revolving loans use Base Rate plus 2.75% or Term SOFR plus 3.75%. Term SOFR has a 1.00% floor, the Base Rate a 2.00% floor, and interest on the loans is payable solely in cash.

Both facilities mature on the fifth anniversary of the effective date. A springing provision can move maturity to 91 days before Tempus’s 0.75% convertible senior notes due 2030 unless those notes are repaid or converted first or specified liquidity requirements are met.

It has been revealed that certain Tempus subsidiaries will guarantee the obligations, which are secured by substantially all assets of Tempus and those subsidiaries. The agreement includes minimum-liquidity and minimum-revenue covenants. Revolving availability depends on eligible accounts receivable and certain qualified cash, subject to reserves and other limitations, and revolving interest can be charged on a minimum balance even when actual borrowings are lower.

According to recent reports, the cash election uses flexibility described in Tempus’s July 20, 2026 acquisition announcement. The merger agreement priced Personalis at $16.25 per common share, representing approximately $1.5 billion in enterprise value net of Tempus’s existing ownership. Consideration was originally structured as all stock, with Tempus holding an option to pay cash capped at 50% of the consideration and a floating exchange ratio capped at 0.3356 Tempus shares per Personalis share.

In a recent development, the cash estimate assumes 108,740,631 Personalis shares outstanding immediately before closing and no perfected appraisal demands. The number of shares designated for cash can automatically decrease, with a corresponding increase in the stock portion, to satisfy the merger agreement’s reorganization threshold, determined using Tempus’s closing-date trading price.

Tempus states the acquisition pairs its multimodal data, AI capabilities and commercial infrastructure with Personalis’s tumor-informed molecular residual disease (MRD) technology, including the NeXT Personal test, which detects small traces of circulating tumor DNA to monitor treatment response, residual cancer and recurrence.

The transaction builds on a partnership established in November 2023, through which Tempus invested in Personalis and commercialized NeXT Personal. Tempus CEO Eric Lefkofsky called MRD “a large and rapidly growing market” and mentioned the collaboration had demonstrated the strength of combining Personalis’s technology with his firm’s commercial infrastructure.

Sources indicate that tempus originally expected the acquisition to close in late 2026 or early 2027. Closing remains subject to Personalis stockholder adoption of the merger agreement and other customary conditions. Tempus has now aligned the debt package with its cash-and-stock election, but the borrowing timetable and the proposed AI-supported MRD expansion both remain tied to completion of the acquisition.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lvignoli

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • It has been revealed that the above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

It has been revealed that the above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

Our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

Recent findings suggest that this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

According to recent reports, this checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

This defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

We now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

Industry observers note that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

This part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

In a recent development, index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

According to recent reports, the return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

Sources indicate that still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

Sources indicate that as for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.

📅 08 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code.
  • In a recent development, the format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Recent findings suggest that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

In a recent development, the format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

It has been revealed that what we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

Sources indicate that we want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of owners, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

The coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

Recent findings suggest that we're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

In a recent development, if you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an problem, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Industry observers note that will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fireworks AI made Tencent’s open-weight Hy4 Flash available on its serverless API on November 25, 2026, pricing the Standard tier at $0.07 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens. The announcement adds benchmark tests that position the model as a low-cost option for professional and agentic work.

Cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. A Priority tier is also available, and the service is served globally. Developers can instead use on-demand dedicated GPUs; the Hy4 Flash model page lists function calling as supported and fine-tuning and embeddings as unsupported.

Hy4 Flash uses a mixture-of-experts design, in which only about 12 billion of its roughly 220 billion parameters are active for each token. It accepts text and image input. The native context window is 1M tokens, while Fireworks is serving 512K at launch, a material constraint for applications built around very long documents or extended agent sessions.

It has been revealed that tencent introduced Hy4 Flash on November 16, 2026, as its most cost-effective Hy model for everyday productivity and released the weights on GitHub, Hugging Face, ModelScope, and AtomGit. Tencent states reinforcement learning reduced average end-to-end output tokens by 50%, while megakernels, 4-bit quantization, and DFly lifted decoding speed beyond 150 tokens per second.

According to recent reports, fireworks reports testing the model on seven professional benchmarks with the same harness used for other models on each leaderboard, at high reasoning. Costs are based on recorded tokens at Fireworks’ serverless prices, and the results are dated November 22, 2026. Hy4 Flash reached the score-cost Pareto frontier on every board where cost was recorded, meaning no listed model delivered a higher score at a lower cost.

Fireworks’ run of Epiq’s CorporateBench, which tests questions across thousands of internal firm emails and meeting notes, produced a 75.9% score for Hy4 Flash: sixth of 14 models and slightly above Claude Opus 5.5’s 75.4%. The respective costs were $0.013 and $2.80 per task.

Rogo’s Big Finance Benchmark produced a 49.2% tie with Claude Opus 5 in Fireworks’ tests, at $0.0065 per task for Hy4 Flash versus $1.83 for Opus 5. Hy4 Flash also placed above Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1 Pro, which each scored 48.2%. GPT-6 Luna was the only cheaper model on that board, but scored 35.3%.

On Sierra’s τ³-Banking agent benchmark, Fireworks reports a 49.2% score for Hy4 Flash against 49.1% for Claude Opus 5. The cost was $0.012 per trial versus $2.59. Across all boards where it recorded cost, Fireworks found Hy4 Flash was the lowest-cost model except on Substantial Finance.

In a recent development, fireworks’ rankings were weaker elsewhere: Hy4 Flash placed 16th of 18 models on HealthBench Professional and 19th of 22 on DeepSWE. Tencent recommends the larger Hy4 for long-horizon software engineering because of its higher intelligence ceiling, reinforcing that the cost results do not establish uniform superiority across professional work.

Before opening the endpoint, Fireworks ran Hy4 Flash through its launch-validation suite on FireAttention, its inference engine, and compared the results with Tencent’s official endpoint. The company reports that every score came within one point of Tencent’s. The Fireworks results were:.

In a recent development, the deployment’s appeal is therefore workload-specific: Fireworks’ tests pair near-parity with Claude Opus on selected professional tasks with much lower recorded costs, while the reduced hosted context and weaker health and software results set clear limits. Validation against Tencent’s endpoint gives developers a direct reference point for assessing whether Fireworks’ serving configuration preserves the model’s expected behavior.

Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.
  • The first release of Waypoint indicated that real-time generative worlds were possible.
  • Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waypoint-1.5 Weights on the Hub.

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

The first release of Waypoint indicated that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

According to recent reports, on desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that with Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

Recent findings suggest that we also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

Sources indicate that what people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

If world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

There are two ways to play Waypoint-1.5.

Sources indicate that the first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the new installer flow, customers can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems showed that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.
