General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How Love Saves Lives

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable.
  • How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?
  • Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable. At a memorial for one young suicide I attended a few years ago, the father of the deceased could barely walk to the altar to light a candle. Everyone was crying.

How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?

Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger. Severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are all inordinately common among people who die by suicide.

Severe mental illnesses are no doubt responsible for many, if not most, of the eight hundred thousand or so suicides that occur around the world each year, including, perhaps, that young person’s whose memorial I attended.

My book, Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic, isn’t primarily about such cases—or about how to prevent suicide. Such a book would have detailed sections about psychotherapy, restrictions on firearms, safety barriers for bridges, and other measures that really do save lives. Instead, my aim was to explore why some people want to take their own lives in the first place and how that desire might be reduced, in both individuals and communities.

Recent findings suggest that having spent the past few years reading about suicide, speaking with scores of people who’ve experienced suicidal feelings, and having experienced them myself from time to time, I’ve come to understand that what suicidal people feel is the indifference, not of the universe, but of those closest to them. They sense that their own feelings don’t matter to the people they care most about.

These experiences are backed up by studies showing that the main reason suicidal people want to die is because they think no one cares about them. Some suicides even seem to believe they’re doing everyone a favor by taking their own lives.

Psychologist Thomas Joiner, who’s been studying suicide for thirty years, calls it a force of nature that distorts people’s minds so they become convinced that they are a burden to others and no one wants them around. In study after study, the most common trigger for suicide is a perceived rupture in a close relationship, either with a lover, parent, or other close relative, that seems irreparable to the suicidal person.

Recent findings suggest that given that suicide seems driven by fraught or broken connections, it’s perhaps not surprising that I also discovered that suicide can spread within social groups like a disease. The suicide rate of particular groups can jump—sometimes increasing three- or four-fold or more—in a short time, meaning it behaves like an epidemic, like malaria during the rainy season or flu in the fall. Suicide epidemics unfold more slowly than these microbial plagues—over years or decades, not weeks or months—but they happen far too promptly to result from genetic changes, and affect far too many people to be explained away as spontaneous cases of biologically caused mental illness or brain injury. The causes therefore must have something to do with the changing social environment in which these people live. Suicide epidemics have occurred on virtually every continent.

What’s scary about this is that it means suicide could come for any of us. The very existence of suicide epidemics proves that people with suicidal feelings aren’t a species apart. Anyone can feel suicidal under certain conditions—and the key to stopping suicide epidemics is to change those conditions.

Sources indicate that I teach and write about public health and have long been fascinated by epidemics because they always tell a story. In most literary depictions of epidemics, such as Albert Camus’s The Plague or Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of the Plague Year, they seem to strike from nowhere, but this isn’t how epidemics typically behave. Individual cases of disease are hard to predict. Some of us will become ill tomorrow, but there’s no telling who. Even those who take risks may well escape the consequences.

What might cause a suicide epidemic?

According to recent reports, first, it’s crucial to understand what doesn’t. Suicide isn’t more common during wars or where people are poorer or have recently experienced some environmental disaster like a flood, earthquake, or wildfire. Suicide was common among African slaves, especially on the ships en route to America and when they first arrived, but despite segregation, police brutality, mass incarceration, and other outrages, the suicide rate of African Americans has been generally lower than that of U.S. whites since record-keeping began in the 1930s.

What seems to matter is whether people believe someone, somewhere, really cares about and understands them.

Sources indicate that the mental pain that drives suicide is really the flip side of love, indicates Israeli neuroscientist Yoram Yovell. “It probably evolved along with motherhood. . . . Inherent in us are very strong emotional forces that function to keep mothers and babies together. When they get too far from each other, they feel mental pain,” which we experience when we search for love. This is why “so many children’s stories are about a boy looking for his lost mother.”.

It has been revealed that evidence supports Yovell’s theory. A 1999 study found that some 78% of high lethality suicide attempters had recently experienced the loss of a close personal relationship, and suicide notes often express love for those left behind. In 2012, Zimri Yaseen and his colleagues reported that suicidal people interviewed in emergency rooms were especially likely to report that in the three preceding days, they’d felt “unusually intense or deep feelings of love,” which they presumably also felt were not reciprocated.

Sources indicate that but why would large groups of people—from the islands of Micronesia to the Arctic Circle, from the cities of post-communist Russia to the towns of contemporary America—suddenly begin questioning their most intimate attachments? How does love suddenly disappear—or seem to—from the lives of thousands of people?

In my book, Why Live, I argue that it has to do with how we internalize socioeconomic change.

Industry observers note that the first well-researched suicide epidemic occurred across Western Europe during the 19th century. Intellectuals debated the causes as we debate the vicissitudes of the stock market. Rising suicide rates were attributed to socialism, atmospheric moisture, the vice of masturbation, and the Romantic era inclination to preserve—through death—the passions of youth against the onslaught of Bourgeois boredom brought on by industrialization and urban life.

According to recent reports, doctors even searched, in vain, for a “suicidogenic” organ in the cadavers of people who’d died by suicide. But others blamed society, that collective property of human groups that shapes our thinking and behavior.

As a Jew growing up in France amid increasing anti-Semitism, Émile Durkheim had seen how shared values and beliefs buffered his people against the effects of discrimination and how anti-Semitism tightened bonds among them. He went on to become one of the founders of sociology, which is the study of those bonds: what holds us together, what drives us apart, and what happens as a result.

In his 1897 book, Suicide, Durkheim theorized that suicides increase wherever society is fragmenting and people are growing more detached from one another: where divorce rates are higher, for example, and where Protestants, with their individualistic culture and aloofness from collective ritual, outnumber Catholics. He likened it to entropy—the universal tendency toward chaos and disorder at the atomic level discovered by physicists earlier in the century. Appearing on the eve of humanity’s, as yet, bloodiest century, Durkheim’s book seemed to foreshadow the trouble to come.

What is it about fragmenting societies that causes mental pain?

Durkheim was vague, even a little loopy, when it came to explaining this. At the time, psychologists were just discovering the unconscious, which they explored through studies of hypnosis and hallucinations. Durkheim followed this research closely, and believed that values and meanings flowed through populations like electrical currents, as if societies had what scholars Laurent Mucchielli and Marc Renneville refer to as a “collective soul.” These currents could change people’s behavior through unconscious mechanisms, just as changes in temperature and pressure change the behavior of molecules.

Many late-19th-century scientists believed that our brains generated signals analogous to radio waves. Alexander Graham Bell, Nikola Tesla, and James Clerk Maxwell even wired up helmets and other gizmos to try to measure them. Mark Twain told Harper’s Monthly that thoughts could shoot from brain to brain, without their owners having to open their mouths to communicate. Likewise, Durkheim maintained that whatever suicidal people said about their feelings were just expressions of resolutions planted in their minds by the vibes of a disintegrating society.

Recent findings suggest that the brain-wave theory eventually fell out of fashion. In the 1930s, one of Durkheim’s protégés came closer to explaining the psychological effects of social fragmentation. Maurice Halbwachs taught at the University of Strasbourg from 1919 until his death in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945. His 1930 monograph The Causes of Suicide identified an existential loneliness that, if not entirely upcoming, flourished in the growing towns and cities of 19th-century Europe and the countryside they engulfed.

According to Halbwachs, cities create opportunities for social and economic advancement, but they also create the conditions for exploitative relationships, swindles, romantic betrayals, fragile friendships, broken families, unstable jobs, and many other sources of despair.

As European cities grew, so did a latest class of people who were particularly prone to suicide, including abandoned lovers, lonely widowers, workers who’d lost their jobs, nobles shamed by some dishonorable act, gamblers who couldn’t pay their debts, merchants who’d ruined themselves, heirs who’d squandered their fortunes, and others who’d suffered a common bitter fate: sudden exclusion from a cherished social community. As Halwachs writes:.

Industry observers note that they all see their social level lowered. They are to a certain extent declassed. But what does it mean to be declassed? It is to pass from a group that one knows, that esteems you, to another that ignores you and whose appreciation one has no reason to hold. One then feels a void opening around oneself. Those who once surrounded you, with whom you had so many ideas in common, so many prejudices in common, with whom so many affinities brought you together because you found yourself in them as they found yourself in you, suddenly move away. You disappear from their concerns and their memory. Those among whom you find yourself understand neither your disorientation, nor your nostalgia and your regrets. Detached from the group by a sudden shock, you are incapable, or at least you believe yourself incapable, of ever finding in another any support, nor anything to replace what you have lost.

In the midst of the 19th-century suicide crisis, the very meaning of the word “lonely” changed, from an adjective typically used to describe empty places and people who stood alone before God to one with the emotional and psychological connotations it has for us today. Suicidal despair, Halbwachs wrote, had been rarer in the past because traditional rural life was simpler and more predictable:.

In a recent development, we lived on the spot . . . adapted to each other, knowing each other too well to be frequently exposed to the clashes that occur when we move from one place, one situation, one profession, to another. Business carried less risk. Ambitions were less aroused, humiliations rarer. We thought and felt in common. Sorrows and troubles, instead of concentrating within the consciousness of this or that individual, dispersed and died out within the group.

What Halbwachs was describing was the transition from what German sociologist Ferdinand Tönnies called Gemeinschaft, or communities based on trust, mutual respect, and sharing of whatever material goods one had, to Gesellschaft, societies based largely on market transactions and political calculation in which ties of friendship and loyalty are relegated to private family life, and may not even reliably be found there.

As far as I’ve been able to determine, wherever that transition has occurred, a suicide epidemic has followed swiftly behind.

In a recent development, but there is another ingredient, too. As villagers shifted away from subsistence and small-scale farming to wage labor and trade, their intimate relationships became both more fragile and more precious. The extended family, which once formed a social mesh that supported everyone, waned in significance, and walls rose up around increasingly private and nuclearized families, usually dominated by a single, generally male breadwinner, upon whom everyone else in the family depended. If you felt your family didn’t respect and care about you, you were in a new sort of trouble, not just because the community no longer offered you a livelihood, but because your whole identity was at stake.

Sources indicate that modern capitalist society creates, in all of us, something of the double consciousness described by the great African American sociologist W. E. B. DuBois. When a modern person looks at a stranger, he wonders not only, as his villager ancestors did, “What can I do to help this person? And is he the kind of person who will help me?” but “What does that stranger see when he looks at me? What essence does he detect? A beauty or a beast? A success or a failure? A respectable person or a fool?”.

According to recent reports, the answer sometimes comes as a disappointment. In traditionally cohesive societies, this mattered less, because a person’s worth was measured by what he did for others, and everyone was capable of contributing something. You might not be the best hunter, fisherman, storyteller, or drummer; you might not be the best grower of breadfruit or builder of igloos; but you still mattered. Only the greedy and selfish were looked down upon and excluded.

In modern societies, generosity still counts, but for far less than it used to. If others find us wanting—because of our looks, talents, graces, bank accounts, intelligence, or for whatever reason—we are alone with it, and must make sense of it, somehow.

For most of us, what makes modern life, with all its loneliness and insecurity, bearable are close relationships with people we count on to see and accept us for who we really are—whatever our flaws. Romantic rejection is exquisitely painful because we feel that that special quality within us, the thing that makes us lovable—and everyone has something—has either been unrecognized or, worse, seen and rejected.

The pain of rejection by a parent or other close relative is even worse because it can make us feel as though no one could ever understand and sympathize with us. After all, they know us best of all.

In the absence of an abstract sense of group belonging, interpersonal love, especially between parents and children and romantic partners, has become the main source of our psychological resilience, our ability to withstand the disappointments encountered in the outside world, just as the mutually reinforcing group gave strength to our ancestors fighting for survival on the plains, tundras, beaches, and forests of the past.

Love is not just a feeling; it’s also a culture, which developed fairly recently, first in Western societies, and then around the world on the heels of capitalism, modernity, and individualism. It’s no coincidence, the social philosopher Erich Fromm pointed out, that as modern ways of life displaced the traditional, cohesive village and clan, love poems, songs, and stories came to occupy the center of Western culture, displacing archaic tales of heroism and godliness.

It’s not that love was absent from the art of the ancient past, but as often as not, it was seen as a cause of calamity and human folly. Think of Helen of Troy, Dido and Aeneas, Adam and Eve. Then, more or less in lockstep with commercial culture and urbanization, love came to be seen as a force superior to the gods or God or honor or historic destiny.

The behavior of parents and spouses changed, too. Until the 1800s, childrearing in England, for example, was seen as an exercise less in nurturing than in training for adulthood. Men who were fed up with their wives could sell them at markets or abandon them and marry someone else without divorcing. Infants who died weren’t even listed in parish registers. Only in the 19th century did heartfelt observations of sons and daughters begin appearing regularly in the diaries of American and English mothers.

Industry observers note that with the growth of markets and formal state institutions, people came to rely less on kinship networks for social welfare and trade and the family gradually shifted from an economic enterprise to a child-centered haven in a heartless world. The 1700s saw the first toy shops, women’s magazines, popular child care manuals, and family portraits. Christian churches, which had previously stressed family discipline and sometimes even the virtues of wife-beating, now promoted ideals of conjugal and parental love.

It has been revealed that today, birthday parties, children’s allowances, and Valentine’s Day cards are symbols we use to assure each other that our most key relationships are real. Meanwhile, parenting manuals, happily-ever-after fairy tales, Hollywood movies, and the novels of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Charles Dickens, Barbara Cartland, Colleen Hoover, and countless others illustrate the enactment of love according to Western norms.

Premodern Europeans, as well as Indigenous groups the world over, didn’t need this culture because in the mutual aid communities of bygone days, you knew who you were and what you needed to do to gain the esteem of others: You had to pitch in for the group. You helped others and they helped you. That was love, and according to accounts of anthropologists, it was everywhere, as ubiquitous as air.

Sources indicate that but when these groups modernized, in some cases very rapidly under the forces of capitalism and colonialism, the rules changed. Now it was unclear what the common goals were and what others were looking for in us. If they didn’t like us, there wasn’t a lot we could do about it. If the people we loved—our romantic partners, parents, and children—felt that way, it was intolerably painful because our hearts had nowhere to turn. Every rejection could now elicit devastating feelings of aloneness. “Who am I?” we are left to wonder. “Am I worth anything at all to anyone?”.

Signifiers of love—birthday cards and so on—aren’t enough. We need the confidence that our own feelings are understood. Some people, either because of the distortions of mental illness or because they really are lost and alone, simply don’t have it.

Industry observers note that but all is not lost. As I argue in Why Live, communities can regrow, just like decimated forests. The best policy I can think of is to strive for greater economic equality, which will naturally reduce insecurity, and, in turn, foster greater spiritual as well as material generosity. We are kinder to one another when we don’t feel threatened. Otherwise, the best advice I can think of is not to make things worse. When positive communities begin to emerge, the trick is not to ruin them.

Sources indicate that let’s treat communities like ecosystems so that every time a major economic policy shift is proposed—a massive new trade deal or development project—the effects on communities are considered, and the preservation of Gemeinschaft is prioritized. Ideally, studies of this, analogous to the environmental impact studies now required by all World Bank loans to developing countries, would be conducted with the full and meaningful involvement of affected communities.

Some elements of Gemeinschaft survive, even in these harsh times—in well-functioning neighborhoods, in friendship networks, sometimes in the military, and in some schools and workplaces. You know it when you see it; it’s where you feel your dignity is recognized. In defending and building that, we give everyone more reason to live.

Helen C. Epstein, Ph.D., is visiting professor of global public health and human rights at Bard College. She is the author of Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic and Another Fine Mess: America, Uganda, and the War on Terror.

#126439. Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

Shipping a Trillion Parameters With a Hub Bucket: Delta Weight Sync in TRL

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.
  • Sources indicate that if you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline.
  • In a recent development, the inference engine speaks the policy of step N.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

Sources indicate that if you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

In a recent development, the inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

In a recent development, fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you upgrade your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

Cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:.

The only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

In a recent development, before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An enhancement gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

In a recent development, now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the upgrade to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​.

The normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the update.

In other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The patch gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

In a recent development, this is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam update, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

In a recent development, we do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:.

That is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

According to recent reports, under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:.

In a recent development, the property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

Sources indicate that the trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

In a recent development, now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

In a recent development, we picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

A few nice consequences of this choice:.

The cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each new inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

Recent findings suggest that the trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:.

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

Sources indicate that this is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the fresh _sync_weight flow are:.

Sources indicate that the line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

Sources indicate that vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:.

Industry observers note that we register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

It has been revealed that worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

One honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

Recent findings suggest that this is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:.

According to recent reports, setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:.

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:.

The trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

A few things, and we think they are substantial.

Sources indicate that async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

Take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

It has been revealed that what does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

In a recent development, now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

It has been revealed that we are not pretending this is finished. Here is the honest list.

Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.
  • Recent findings suggest that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference.
  • It has been revealed that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Recent findings suggest that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

It has been revealed that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:.

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Industry observers note that figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry.

In a recent development, we trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

In a recent development, we then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

According to recent reports, figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison demonstrates the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

It has been revealed that A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

Industry observers note that naViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

In a recent development, figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 demonstrates three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:.

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

According to recent reports, double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass.

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

According to recent reports, in the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

In a recent development, the worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

According to recent reports, RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Industry observers note that figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States.
  • But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the United States. That is about 17% of all US households — roughly 1 in 6. And the number is growing: the US added over 2 million newly introduced millionaire households between 2019 and 2022 alone, even through a global pandemic.

But here is what might surprise you: most millionaires do not look like what you expect. They are not driving Ferraris or living in mansions. The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently demonstrates that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

Recent findings suggest that this matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. It is about consistent behavior applied over time. And if you are on the FI path, you are following the exact same playbook that created 22 million millionaires.

The exact number depends on how you measure it and which data source you use:.

Industry observers note that the discrepancy between 22 million and 14-15 million comes down to whether you include home equity. If you count total net worth (including home equity), approximately 22 million households qualify. If you count only investable assets (excluding the primary residence), the number drops to about 14-15 million.

It has been revealed that for FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Note: Growth includes both newly introduced wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (the largest ever conducted) surveyed over 10,000 millionaires and found: 79% received zero inheritance. The top occupations were engineer, accountant, teacher, management, and attorney — not entrepreneurs or celebrities. 96% remarked anyone can become a millionaire with discipline and consistent investing. The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Sources: Chris Hogan National Study of Millionaires, Thomas Stanley "The Millionaire Next Door", Federal Reserve SCF.

The path to millionaire status in America overwhelmingly follows a formula, not a lottery ticket:.

Millionaires are not "the 1%" — they are the top 10-15%. Here is how wealth is distributed across US households:.

Source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022.

This means approximately 16% of American households have a net worth of $1 million or more. And the pathway from $500K-$1M (where 11% of households sit) to the millionaire club is often just a matter of continuing to do what they are already doing for another 5-10 years.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):.

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:.

Recent findings suggest that A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

Recent findings suggest that if you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:.

According to recent reports, the standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as promptly as possible.

It has been revealed that the data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

Industry observers note that the data notes this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

It has been revealed that multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

According to recent reports, set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

Industry observers note that 73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

In a recent development, overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement prepares (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Industry observers note that yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

According to recent reports, there are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by fresh technology, global crises, and loneliness.
  • Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing.
  • In a recent development, the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by fresh technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

In a recent development, joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway noted, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:.

In a recent development, the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

While wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

According to recent reports, psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”.

In a recent development, perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, stated Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”.

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”.

For young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:.

Our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

According to recent reports, iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she remarked, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”.

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

According to recent reports, “Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes said. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”.

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

Joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas noted.

Industry observers note that clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:.

We have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, said Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

“Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so important,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”.

Even technology has a role to play, Mattu remarked. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

Industry observers note that he suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:.

According to recent reports, we start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Katherine Reynolds Lewis is the special projects editor at the Greater Good Science Center and author of the Good News About Bad Behavior. She is an award-winning science journalist with bylines in the Atlantic, Fortune, Latest York Times, Undark, and Washington Post.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Processing shouldn't be the first thing that happens.
  • Imagine selecting a PDF, waiting for processing, and finally receiving an error saying the file was encrypted.
  • Or finding out that the selected document wasn't actually a PDF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Processing shouldn't be the first thing that happens.

Imagine selecting a PDF, waiting for processing, and finally receiving an error saying the file was encrypted.

Or discovering that the file was corrupted.

Or finding out that the selected document wasn't actually a PDF.

Some of these problems could have been identified earlier.

Validate before doing expensive work.

A useful file-processing workflow should perform basic checks before starting its main operation.

Is its size within the application's supported limits?

Does its content resemble the expected file format?

Does the requested operation support its structure?

One important detail: checking a filename extension or MIME type alone isn't sufficient.

A more meaningful validation process examines the actual file contents and attempts to parse the document.

Validation isn't the same as guaranteeing success.

Even when initial checks pass, processing can still fail.

A PDF might contain unusual structures, unsupported encryption, malformed objects, or features that a particular library doesn't handle.

That's why validation should be followed by proper error handling.

"This PDF appears to be password-protected. Please provide an unlocked document.".

The second message gives the user something actionable.

Similarly, distinguish between:.

File exceeding supported limits.

The exact messages depend on what the application can reliably identify.

Build for the files people actually have.

Users don't prepare documents specifically to make your application happy.

They bring old scans, exported reports, unusual forms, and files created by software you've never tested.

A good file utility needs to expect that.

What's your preferred approach to file validation: lightweight checks before processing, or a more comprehensive validation stage?

#126418. The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.
